name: Re-ranking with Cross-Encoders
question: Are the best passages at the top, not just somewhere in the pool?
summary: A second stage after retrieval. Fast search, dense or hybrid, fetches a wide candidate set such as the top 50; a cross-encoder then reads the query and each candidate together and scores how well the passage answers it, and only the top few reach the prompt. Reading both texts together is far more precise than comparing two separate vectors, but it costs time per candidate, and it can only reorder what the first stage found.
useCases: Help centres and knowledge bases where the top 3 to 5 decide the answer
Hindi, Hinglish and mixed-language queries (with a multilingual model)
Pipelines that must say “not found” instead of guessing

items.detail: how many first-stage results to score, often 30–100
how many reach the prompt, often 3–8
cross-encoder, multilingual cross-encoder or LLM re-ranker
grows with candidates and passage length

ColBERT-style models sit between bi- and cross-encoders

Score every candidate with a cross-encoder, multilingual if users mix languages
Keep the top 3 to 8 above a score threshold
Measure recall at the kept depth and p95 latency together

steps.title: Retrieve wide and cheap
steps.text: Hybrid search returns 50 candidates in about 40 ms. For “GST invoice kaise download karun?” the right help article is in the pool, but at rank 17.

steps.title: See why the first stage misses
steps.text: A bi-encoder embeds the query and each article separately and compares two vectors. The article titled “Tax documents for sellers” never shares the question’s words.

steps.title: Read query and passage together
steps.text: A cross-encoder scores each (query, passage) pair jointly, attending across both texts. A multilingual model such as bge-reranker-v2-m3 handles the Hinglish.

steps.title: Sort by the new score
steps.text: The right article scores 0.94 and moves from rank 17 to rank 1. Articles that merely share words drop.

steps.title: Keep the few, above a threshold
steps.text: Only the top 5 with a score of at least 0.20 reach the prompt. If none qualify, the bot says it could not find the answer instead of guessing.

steps.title: Tune the depth on your data
steps.text: Recall at 5 rises from 0.64 to 0.86 for about 110 ms more at 50 candidates. Deeper pools add recall slowly and latency linearly.

Works on top of any retriever
A score threshold lets the system decline instead of guessing

cons: Adds latency that grows with candidates and passage length

playgroundGuide.scenario: Vyapar Mart, a fictional marketplace, answers seller questions from 8,000 help articles. 200 test questions: 140 in English and 60 in Hinglish, plus 20 that the help centre cannot answer. Hybrid search takes 40 ms and the latency budget is 500 ms.
controls: Choose the re-ranker: none, English cross-encoder, multilingual cross-encoder or an LLM re-ranker.
Drag how many candidates are scored and how many passages are kept.
Switch on the score threshold that lets the bot say “not found”.

outputs.meaning: Questions with the right article among the passages kept, overall and for Hinglish.

outputs.name: Latency
outputs.meaning: Search plus re-ranking, against the 500 ms budget.

outputs.name: No-answer questions declined
outputs.meaning: Of the 20 the help centre cannot answer.

presets.name: No re-ranker
presets.expect: About 56% recall at 5 in 40 ms; every no-answer question still gets an answer.

presets.name: English cross-encoder, 50 candidates
presets.expect: About 78% overall, but Hinglish only 63%; 115 ms.

presets.name: Multilingual, 100 candidates, threshold
presets.expect: About 85% overall and 83% Hinglish in 290 ms; 16 of 20 no-answer questions declined.

presets.name: LLM re-ranker, 100 candidates
presets.expect: About 87% recall, but 1,740 ms: far over budget.

Show that re-ranking cannot rescue passages the first stage never retrieved.

Choose candidate depth by recall and latency together

practice.scenario: Vyapar Mart, a fictional marketplace, answers seller questions from 8,000 help articles, many asked in Hinglish. Hybrid search fetches 100 candidates in about 40 ms; a multilingual cross-encoder scores each against the question, and only the top 5 scoring at least 0.20 reach the model. If none qualify, the bot says it could not find the answer.

industries.use: Seller and buyer help centres in several languages
Product FAQs where the top answer must be the right one
Intranet search over policies, wikis and tickets

practice.analogy: A recruiter and an interviewer. The recruiter skims 100 CVs in minutes and shortlists 50; the interviewer spends real time with each one and picks the best five.

library.name: sentence-transformers
library.what: Runs open cross-encoder re-rankers such as BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 locally, on CPU or GPU.

practice.note: The first run downloads the model. Scores are relative; tune the threshold on your own labelled questions.

samples.code:
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

reranker = CrossEncoder("BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3", max_length=512)

query = "GST invoice kaise download karun?"
candidates = [
    "Returns policy: how to accept or reject a customer return.",
    "Tax documents for sellers: download your monthly GST invoice from Payments > Reports.",
    "Seller fees: commission and shipping charges by category.",
]
scores = reranker.predict([(query, c) for c in candidates])
for score, text in sorted(zip(scores, candidates), reverse=True):
    print(f"{score:.2f}  {text}")

numericDrill.question: Search takes 40 ms and a cross-encoder takes 2.5 ms per candidate. What is the total latency for re-ranking 100 candidates, in milliseconds?
numericDrill.answer: 40 + 100 × 2.5 = 290 ms. Scoring 200 candidates would take 540 ms, over a 500 ms budget.

interview.question: When is a re-ranker worth adding?
interview.answer: When the right passage is usually retrieved but not in the top few. Measure recall at 50 and recall at 5: a large gap means re-ranking will help; a low recall at 50 means fix retrieval first.

interview.question: Cross-encoder or LLM re-ranker?
interview.answer: Cross-encoders are fast and precise enough for most pipelines, at a few milliseconds per candidate on a GPU. LLM re-rankers can reason about harder relevance but add hundreds of milliseconds to seconds; use them offline, for small candidate sets, or where latency does not matter.

mistakes.mistake: Re-ranking only the top 5 that will be kept
mistakes.fix: Score a wide pool, then keep the few

mistakes.mistake: Using an English re-ranker for Hinglish users
mistakes.fix: Use a multilingual model and report recall per language

quiz.question: What does a cross-encoder do that a bi-encoder does not?
options: Reads the query and a passage together to score relevance
quiz.explanation: Joint reading gives more precise relevance, at more cost per pair.

quiz.question: Recall at 50 is 92% and recall at 5 is 58%. What will help most?
quiz.explanation: The right passage is usually retrieved but ranked too low: a re-ranking problem.

quiz.question: Recall at 50 is 45%. Will a re-ranker fix it?
options: No: it can only reorder what was retrieved; fix retrieval first
quiz.explanation: Re-ranking cannot add passages to the pool.

quiz.question: Search takes 40 ms and re-ranking 2.5 ms per candidate. What is total latency for 100 candidates?
Users write in Hinglish. Which re-ranker?
options: A multilingual cross-encoder such as bge-reranker-v2-m3
quiz.explanation: English-only models score code-mixed queries poorly.

quiz.question: Which are reasons to use a score threshold after re-ranking? Select all that apply.
options: Let the system say “not found” when nothing is relevant
Avoid sending weak passages to the model
Reduce hallucinated answers on unanswerable questions
Make scores comparable across all corpora
quiz.explanation: Scores are not universally calibrated; tune the threshold per corpus.

quiz.question: Why not run a cross-encoder over the whole corpus?
options: It must score every query–document pair at query time, which is far too slow
quiz.explanation: Cross-encoders cannot precompute document vectors.

quiz.question: An LLM re-ranker takes 900 ms plus 8 ms per candidate. For 100 candidates, what is its latency?
quiz.explanation: 900 + 100 × 8 = 1,700 ms, too slow for most live chat.

quiz.question: Where does ColBERT-style late interaction sit?
options: Between bi-encoders and cross-encoders in precision and cost
quiz.explanation: Token-level matching with precomputed document embeddings.

quiz.question: Which should you measure when tuning candidate depth? Select all that apply.
options: The number of GPUs in the data centre
quiz.explanation: Quality and latency together, sliced by segment.

quiz.question: A re-ranker keeps the top 5 of 5 candidates. What is wrong?
options: It reorders the same 5 it would keep anyway; retrieve a wider pool
quiz.explanation: Score a wide pool, keep a few.

quiz.question: Re-ranking 200 candidates takes 540 ms against a 500 ms budget. What do you try first?
options: Score about 100 candidates and check recall
quiz.explanation: Recall usually changes little between 100 and 200, while latency doubles.

quiz.question: Cross-encoder scores for two different queries are 0.4 and 0.9. What can you conclude?
options: The second answer is more than twice as likely to be right
Little: scores rank passages within a query, not across queries
The first query should be dropped
Nothing is relevant for the first query
quiz.explanation: Treat scores as rankings; tune thresholds on labelled data.

quiz.question: Which input format does a cross-encoder take?
quiz.explanation: It scores one pair at a time, batched for speed.

quiz.question: After adding a re-ranker, answers improve but costs rise because the prompt still carries 20 passages. What should change?
options: Keep only the top 3 to 8 after re-ranking
quiz.explanation: The point of re-ranking is to send fewer, better passages.

quiz.question: Which are hosted or open re-rankers? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: HNSW is an index, not a re-ranker.

quiz.question: Recall at 5 rises from 64% to 86% with re-ranking. How many more of 500 questions have the right passage in the top 5?
Why might a re-ranker hurt some queries?
options: A domain or language mismatch can push good passages down; evaluate per segment
quiz.explanation: Measure by segment, not just overall.

quiz.question: Long passages are truncated at 512 tokens by the re-ranker. What is the risk?
options: The relevant sentence may be beyond the cut, so the passage scores low
quiz.explanation: Keep chunks within the re-ranker’s window, or use a long-context re-ranker.

quiz.question: Which question does re-ranking answer?
options: Did we retrieve the right passage at all?
Are the best passages at the top of what we retrieved?
quiz.explanation: Ordering, not recall.
